segments_en: Se'if katan 12. Some emend the text to read: 'Regarding the Minchah prayer, everyone agrees that the tamid precedes the incense, as stated in Yoma; but the passage of the meal offering can be recited after the incense.' In truth, if this is the emendation, the words 'unlike Olat Shabbat' are imprecise. Olat Shabbat itself writes this in disagreement with the Shulchan Aruch, which places the tamid and then the incense. Olat Shabbat writes: 'It appears to me that this is not the order; rather, the tamid is followed by the meal offering and then the incense.' Magen Avraham should therefore have said: 'Olat Shabbat writes that the meal offering should precede, etc., but this does not appear correct, for Abaye, etc.' The phrase 'unlike Olat Shabbat' implies that it follows from Magen Avraham's preceding words that Olat Shabbat is wrong, as is Magen Avraham's usual style. It appears to me as follows. Olat Shabbat's words require explanation: why does he place the passage of the meal offering before the incense? His reference to Rambam's Hilchot Temidin supplies nothing, and no one disputes the explicit Talmudic rule that burning the incense preceded the meal offering. It appears that Olat Shabbat also holds that our recitation of the tamid passage corresponds to the limbs. Although the incense preceded the limbs, we nevertheless recite the tamid passage first because it is a type of sacrifice. Since in any case we do not recite the passages in the Temple's sacrificial order, the meal-offering passage may be placed beside the tamid passage, because the meal offering also belongs to the category of offerings, unlike the incense. Although the incense preceded the meal offering, we are already not following the order; otherwise the incense would also have to be recited before the tamid passage, as Hagahot Maimoniyot indeed states. According to Magen Avraham, however, reciting the tamid passage corresponds to the tamid's blood. The recitation consequently follows the sacrificial order, and it is obvious that the order may not be changed: the incense must precede the meal offering. After Magen Avraham concludes that the passage corresponds to the tamid's blood, he writes that at Minchah everyone agrees the tamid comes first, because Yoma states that the afternoon incense came between the limbs and the libations. In any event, the recitation must follow the order, unlike Olat Shabbat, who places the meal offering before the incense because he holds that the tamid passage corresponds to the limbs and that the recitation does not follow the order. This is incorrect, for Abaye arranged it as follows: the tamid's blood preceded the incense, the incense preceded the limbs, and the limbs preceded the meal offering. Whichever way one turns, if the passage corresponds to the limbs, the incense should also precede the tamid passage; one cannot recite them out of order. The atonement is in fact effected by the blood, so our recitation properly follows the order. Understand this carefully.

What remains difficult in my humble opinion is that Magen Avraham and Olat Shabbat discuss the meal offering brought with the morning tamid. What separate meal-offering passage is there? The passage of the libation offering in Parashat Shelach has no relevance to the tamid's meal offering; see there and what my revered grandfather writes in Tevuot Shor. The tamid's meal offering is recited within the tamid passage itself: 'and a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a meal offering.' See the Talmud in Yoma there and Rashi there. It is obviously inconceivable that one should interrupt the passage before 'and a tenth of an ephah' and insert the incense passage in the middle. This certainly cannot be correct and requires further study.

segments_en: He should leave the synagogue. The same applies if he is the only kohen present. He should not raise his hands, but in that case he need not leave the synagogue, since no one calls “Kohanim.” The person who washes the kohanim’s hands should likewise not approach him, and he then does not violate the positive commandment, as explained.

The prayer beginning “Master of the universe” is recited while the kohanim prolong the words with their melody. Some write that not every person should recite this prayer when the kohanim ascend the platform. Rather, only one who dreamed a bad dream that night should recite it. Even if he dreamed on another night during the year, the annulment is effective only on the very day of the dream, just as a fast for a dream is effective specifically on that day. Alternatively, he should omit the two words “I dreamed a dream,” and say instead: “Master of the universe, I am Yours and my dreams are Yours; may it be Your will,” etc. This is from Rosh, chapter Shor Shenagach Es HaParah. This appears correct to me. It is also effective when others dreamed a bad dream concerning him, because he annuls it by saying, “whether dreams that I dreamed or that others dreamed concerning me.” Otherwise, it is improper to recite gratuitous supplications on Shabbos or Yom Tov, because one may not deliberately arouse himself with matters of supplication that break a person’s heart. Prayer and request, however, also include asking Hashem to grant a person abundant gifts beyond his essential needs, and such requests may be made even on Shabbos and Yom Tov. This is why those who arranged the order of the Maamados included additional requests for good on Shabbos. The Levush, authored by Maharam Yaffe, writes, based on Rashi in parashas Va’eschanan, that the Zohar in parashas Naso states as follows: When the chazzan repeats Shemoneh Esrei and there is no Bircas Kohanim, upon saying “May Hashem bless you,” he should face the aron; upon saying “and protect you,” he should turn toward his right. Upon saying “May Hashem illuminate,” he should face the aron; upon saying “His countenance toward you and favor you,” he should turn toward his left, thereby joining it to the right. It is forbidden to delay between washing and the blessing for the time required to walk twenty two amos. The kohanim must therefore wash close to Retzei.

segments_en: The Jew is liable when he tells the non-Jew, “The house is before you; place it wherever you wish.” If, however, he designates for the non-Jew a specific corner within his house in which to place the chametz, he need not remove it, even if he accepted liability for it. Since he lent the non-Jew a specific place, it is regarded as though the chametz is not in the Jew’s domain, and as though he is guarding a non-Jew’s chametz in the non-Jew’s house. This applies when the place was provided without payment. If the Jew rents the place to him for payment, it is forbidden because he profits from an item from which benefit is prohibited. Nevertheless, after the fact, if he accepted the payment, it is permitted for him to benefit from it. This is from Maharam Yaffe.

Even if he later deposited it with another non-Jew, etc. This is from Hagahos Alfasi at the beginning of Pesachim. It appears obvious that if the non-Jew originally placed his chametz in another non-Jew’s domain and the Jew accepted liability for it there, the Jew need not remove it. Beit Yosef writes that if the Jew designated a corner for the non-Jew, he need not remove it, so this case is certainly no more stringent, since the chametz was placed in the non-Jew’s domain from the outset, even though the Jew accepted liability. Many proofs may be brought for this. If the Jew bears no liability, he is not obligated to remove it, but he must place before it a partition ten tefachim high. Even when a specific place was designated for the non-Jew, one should be stringent and require a partition ten tefachim high. Maharitz writes as follows: With due respect to his Torah scholarship, it appears to me that no proof can be brought from that case. There, the owner of the chametz is a Jew. Therefore, there is also a concern in the opposite direction. If the robber does not tell the owner, “Your property is before you,” but instead pays him the value of the chametz, the owner will derive benefit from chametz that remained in existence over Pesach, since he will receive compensation from the robber for it. We therefore say that the robber may tell him, “Your property is before you. Take your chametz.” One might argue that the robber should fulfill the mitzvah of removing chametz, and after destroying it he should become liable to pay, as in a case where the object was lost. There would then be no concern that the owner benefited from the chametz through receiving payment, since the chametz would no longer exist. The answer is that the robber does not wish to do so. Instead, he tells the owner: “The mitzvah of removing the chametz is before you. You fulfill the mitzvah, and your property is before you. I do not wish to pay you money and thereby cause you to benefit through money.” He therefore honors the owner of the chametz with the mitzvah of removing it. That case is unlike ours. Here, if the Jew returns the chametz to the non-Jew, the mitzvah of removing chametz will not be fulfilled. The Jew will benefit by returning the chametz because he will thereby avoid liability to pay. In truth, however, such benefit is not prohibited. Consider this carefully.

segments_en: The wording of the Rambam in chapter 6 of Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin, halachah 2, from the baraita there, as Abaye explains it.

Rashi explains that if he was a bellows-worker or carpenter, one estimates how much a person would accept to desist from such heavy labor and engage in lighter work. This is likewise implied by the Rif. Tosafot explains "an idle worker" as one who is entirely idle and has no other work, estimating how much he would accept to engage in this venture. The Rosh writes likewise. He further writes that here the Sages were lenient regarding rabbinic interest, and a small payment does not appear as interest. The Tur likewise writes this.

segments_en: This too is stated there. He writes that we do not say that because, according to the claimant, he is wicked, he cannot be believed under oath.

The same is written in Choshen Mishpat, siman 82, seif 10. In my humble opinion, this does not disagree with what was written above at the end of siman 169. There, he claims that he took the money permissibly and specifies the basis of permission, namely that he took it through a non-Jew, and he is believed by analogy to the law of a prozbul. Here, however, and in siman 82, he denies everything and does not claim that he took it permissibly, so an oath is administered. As for Rama's words, "and some disagree," I did not merit to see his source in Darkei Moshe.

segments_en: If he gives, etc. There 68b; and Tosafot there s.v. place. And Rashi HaChadash, etc., explained: if they were, etc. And at first glance it implies for the giver's benefit he speaks, that it is included in the principal for the giver; and likewise explained in Tosafot of the Rosh. But Tur explained for the recipient's benefit he speaks, that if the recipient's produce were placed in his possession and the giver gives him money on their account he must assess according to what he would need to give in the market with porter wages; and he wrote: and all the more so if the recipient has, etc., as written in seif 22. And the Rambam explained in another manner, see there.

(Likkut) If, etc. Rashi HaChadash's and Rif's and Shulchan Arukh's version in the baraita: a place where they practiced to raise porter wages for money, they raise for an animal, they raise to raise offspring with his labor wages and his food they raise. And Tosafot there in name of Rashi HaChadash; and Tur explains for the recipient's benefit as in the latter clause. Beit Yosef. And Tur wrote "if he gives," etc., as written here; and he wrote: and even if the iska were in the recipient's house he raises them at the market rate, etc.; and these are two explanations, the first explanation that Tur wrote; and here in Shulchan Arukh it is like the Rambam's explanation; and as Beit Chadash wrote the Rambam's words that whenever the recipient carries to the market to sell the iska, if it is customary to hire, etc., he must give, etc. And the second explanation is Rashi HaChadash's explanation of Tur's words, to carry from the merchandise market when he takes and carries to his house; and the first clause is when he carries to the market; and even though in Tosafot it is written from the giver's house and Tur wrote from the market, all one matter; and Beit Chadash and D.M. explained with one explanation; and in my humble opinion (end).

segments_en: If they stipulated, etc. Rambam; and as written "if half in profit," etc., "if," etc.; and it results that always he takes a sixth of all the wages more than his share which is as a loan; and likewise in loss the giver pays a sixth more which is a third of one of their shares. And the Rambam's teachers wrote that that third is calculated from the giver's share which is the deposit, and it is a third of his share both in wages and in loss; therefore in such a case where it is written here in Shulchan Arukh that they stipulated the dealer shall take a quarter, it results that the deposit share is three parts in loss, the giver pays all. And Ramban and Rashba hold the opposite: that the said third is calculated from the lender's share both in wages and in loss; therefore in such a case the dealer pays a sixth. But in the latter clause where they stipulated a quarter in loss he takes a third in profit which is his share and a third of his share. But the Rambam challenged his teachers that otherwise sometimes the giver will pay more than the loss, for example if they stipulated he take one of seven in profit and the loss is seven dinars, the giver will pay eight dinars and similar; and likewise he challenges Ramban and Rashba that sometimes the dealer will take more than the profit, for example they stipulated the giver lose one of seven and they profited seven dinars, the dealer must take eight dinars; therefore the Rambam explained that if they stipulated on profit, in loss the giver adds a third from his fellow's share which is a loan; and if they stipulated on loss, the dealer takes a third from his fellow's share which is the deposit; and this is what is written "he shall lose," etc., "he shall take," etc.; and likewise is the reasoning: in profit he takes the addition from his fellow's share; and likewise in loss the giver loses the surplus in his fellow's share, therefore we estimate everything according to his fellow's share. But Ramban and Rashba answer the Rambam's difficulty that never does the giver pay more than the loss or the profit; and likewise Choshen Mishpat siman 176 seif 6; and see there siman 93 seif 13 that the Rambam disagrees there and holds he pays from his own house.

(Likkut) If they stipulated, etc. And another method for Semag, and Kesef Mishneh wrote the Rambam's reason: in profit he takes a third more from the deposit share, for that surplus he takes as labor wages on the deposit share; therefore he takes from the deposit share whether much or little according to the deposit share's portion, not so in loss where he takes nothing in profit except that from his labor wages he deducts from his loss so he does not lose so much, he deducts according to the recipient's loss in his share; so much he deducts a third in his loss so he never loses except two-thirds of the recipient's share. And on Beit Yosef siman 176 that incident of half in profit and a third, etc., he does not hold that he should have a sixth extra in wages than in loss but something small; and see there in his words that he explained the Rif's and Rosh's words like the Rambam's and Tur's words, and his words do not appear correct (end).
